claim: Chronic liver disease and cirrhosis are the 11th leading cause of mortality in the United States, accounting for over 40,000 deaths annually.
source: Chronic liver disease and cirrhosis are the 11th leading cause of mortality in the United States, accounting for over 40,000 deaths annually (Murphy et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Murphy et al., 2021

claim: Liver injuries, including those caused by viral infection, excessive alcohol intake, and nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, can lead to fibrosis.
source: Liver injuries, including those caused by viral infection, excessive alcohol intake, and nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, can lead to fibrosis, the accumulation of abnormal scar tissue, in the liver (Bataller and Brenner, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bataller and Brenner, 2005

claim: Liver fibrosis can progress to cirrhosis and end-stage liver disease if left unchecked.
source: If left unchecked, liver fibrosis can progress to cirrhosis and end-stage liver disease (Bataller and Brenner, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bataller and Brenner, 2005

claim: HSC myofibroblasts are the primary cell type responsible for liver fibrosis.
source: HSC myofibroblasts are the primary cell type responsible for liver fibrosis (Friedman et al., 1985; Mederacke et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Friedman et al., 1985 and Mederacke et al., 2013

claim: HSCs reside in the perisinusoidal space and represent 5–8% of total cells in the liver.
source: HSCs reside in the perisinusoidal space and represent 5–8% of total cells in the liver.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the manuscript

claim: In their quiescent, nonfibrotic state, HSCs store vitamin A as retinol ester in lipid droplets.
source: In their quiescent, nonfibrotic state, they store vitamin A as retinol ester in lipid droplets (Geerts, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Geerts, 2001

claim: In response to chronic liver injury, HSCs are activated and trans-differentiate into HSC myofibroblasts, characterized by the loss of lipid droplets, increased contractility, and secretion of ECM proteins.
source: In response to chronic liver injury, HSCs are activated and trans-differentiate into HSC myofibroblasts, characterized by the loss of lipid droplets, increased contractility, and secretion of ECM proteins, leading to fibrosis (Bataller and Brenner, 2005; Friedman, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bataller and Brenner, 2005 and Friedman, 2008

claim: Resolution of liver fibrosis has been observed when the source of liver injury is removed, such as in patients with successful antiviral therapy against hepatitis B or C.
source: Resolution of liver fibrosis has been observed when the source of liver injury is removed, such as in patients with successful antiviral therapy against hepatitis B or C (Benyon and Iredale, 2000; Bonis et al., 2001; Falize et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Benyon and Iredale, 2000; Bonis et al., 2001; Falize et al., 2006

claim: Two mechanisms can contribute to the reduction of activated HSC myofibroblasts during resolution of liver fibrosis: apoptosis of activated HSC myofibroblasts and reversion of HSC myofibroblasts to a more quiescent phenotype.
source: Two mechanisms can contribute to the reduction of activated HSC myofibroblasts during resolution of liver fibrosis – apoptosis of activated HSC myofibroblasts and reversion of HSC myofibroblasts to a more quiescent phenotype (Friedman, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Friedman, 2008

claim: With regression of fibrosis, 40–50% of HSC myofibroblasts revert to an inactive state in vivo, which is associated with reduced collagen expression.
source: With regression of fibrosis, 40–50% of HSC myofibroblasts revert to an inactive state in vivo, which is associated with reduced collagen expression (Kisseleva et al., 2012; Troeger et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kisseleva et al., 2012 and Troeger et al., 2012

claim: There are currently no FDA-approved therapies directed at inhibiting the activity of HSC myofibroblasts.
source: Despite many efforts to understand HSC plasticity and target HSC myofibroblasts, there are currently no FDA-approved therapies directed at inhibiting the activity of HSC myofibroblasts.
evidence: Stated as current state of knowledge

claim: A small molecule screen was developed to identify compounds that promote HSC inactivation.
source: In our previous studies, we developed a small molecule screen to identify compounds that promote HSC inactivation (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2017

claim: A pilot screen revealed the antifibrotic effects of tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs).
source: In a pilot screen, this approach revealed the antifibrotic effects of tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs).
evidence: Stated as a finding from previous work

claim: TCAs inhibit the enzyme acid ceramidase (aCDase).
source: In mechanistic studies, we identified that TCAs inhibit the enzyme acid ceramidase (aCDase).
evidence: Stated as a finding from previous mechanistic studies

claim: Inhibiting aCDase regulates YAP/TAZ-mediated HSC inactivation and reduces fibrogenesis in mouse models and in human precision cut liver slices.
source: In subsequent studies, we demonstrated that inhibiting aCDase regulates YAP/TAZ-mediated HSC inactivation and reduces fibrogenesis in mouse models and in human precision cut liver slices (Alsamman et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alsamman et al., 2020

claim: The screen was expanded approximately 10-fold to include 15,867 experimental wells.
source: Here, we expanded our screen approximately 10-fold to include 15,867 experimental wells and developed a secondary screen to evaluate primary hits.
evidence: Stated as a methodological detail of the current study

claim: Nanchangmycin (NCMC), a polyether ionophore, promotes HSC inactivation.
source: We find that nanchangmycin (NCMC), a polyether ionophore, promotes HSC inactivation.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study

claim: NCMC decreases proliferation, migration, and assembly of collagen fibers in the extracellular matrix.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that NCMC decreases proliferation, migration, and assembly of collagen fibers in the extracellular matrix.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study

claim: Multiple kinases and signaling pathways are involved in mediating the impact of NCMC on HSC activities, including the FYN, PTK2 (FAK) and MAPK1/3 (ERK2/1) pathways.
source: In additional mechanistic studies, we show that multiple kinases and signaling pathways are involved in mediating the impact of NCMC on HSC activities, including the FYN, PTK2 (FAK) and MAPK1/3 (ERK2/1) pathways.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study

claim: 24 compound libraries consisting of 15,867 experimental wells were screened using a high-throughput method to quantify lipid droplet accumulation as an indicator of HSC inactivation.
source: To identify small molecules that induce reversion of HSC myofibroblasts to an inactive phenotype, we screened 24 compound libraries consisting of 15,867 experimental wells using a high-throughput method to quantify lipid droplet accumulation as an indicator of HSC inactivation (Chen et al., 2017; Figure 1A, Supplementary files 1and and 2).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1A and supplementary files, and citation to Chen et al., 2017

claim: Activated HSCs were seeded in 384-well plates, treated with compounds for 48 hr, fixed, and stained with Bodipy to analyze the accumulation of lipid droplets.
source: Activated HSCs were seeded in 384-well plates, treated with compounds for 48 hr, fixed, and stained with Bodipy, a fluorescent lipid dye, to analyze the accumulation of lipid droplets.
evidence: Stated as a methodological detail of the screening approach

claim: DMSO and nortriptyline were included as negative and positive controls, respectively on each plate.
source: DMSO and nortriptyline were included as negative and positive controls, respectively on each plate.
evidence: Stated as a methodological detail of the screening approach

claim: A total of 711 experimental wells, containing 464 different compounds, met the criteria for primary hits.
source: A total of 711 experimental wells, containing 464 different compounds, met these criteria and were identified as primary hits (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1B and Supplementary file 3

claim: The 711 hits were separated into 102 clusters based on their chemical structure.
source: To further narrow the candidate list for secondary screening, the 711 hits were separated into 102 clusters based on their chemical structure, with an average cluster size of seven compounds.
evidence: Stated as a methodological detail of the analysis

claim: 140 unique compounds were included in the secondary screen.
source: In total, 140 unique compounds were included in the secondary screen (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1A and Supplementary file 5

claim: Activated HSCs are characterized by increased expression of α-SMA (encoded by ACTA2) and type 1 collagen (encoded by COL1A1).
source: Activated HSCs are characterized by increased expression of α-SMA (encoded by ACTA2) and type 1 collagen (encoded by COL1A1) (Bataller and Brenner, 2005; Friedman, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bataller and Brenner, 2005 and Friedman, 2008

claim: PSMB2, which encodes proteasome 20 S subunit beta 2, showed the least variation and was chosen as the reference mRNA for the secondary qRT-PCR-based screen.
source: PSMB2, which encodes proteasome 20 S subunit beta 2, showed the least variation as indicated by standard deviation and was chosen as the reference mRNA for the secondary qRT-PCR-based screen (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and data analysis

claim: Of the 140 compounds, 44 compounds met all three criteria for advancement.
source: Of the 140 compounds, a total of 44 compounds met all three criteria.
evidence: Stated as a result of the secondary screen

claim: 39 compounds were advanced for further analysis after excluding 5 compounds that were not commercially available.
source: Five compounds were not commercially available, and 39 compounds were advanced for further analysis.
evidence: Stated as a result of the secondary screen

claim: Of the 39 compounds, 19 received an average score that was the same as or higher than nortriptyline controls.
source: Of the 39 compounds, 19 received an average score that was the same as or higher than nortriptyline controls (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and Table 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and Table 1

claim: NCMC is a natural product of Streptomyces nanchangensis and is a polyether insecticidal antibiotic.
source: Nanchangmycin (NCMC), a natural product of Streptomyces nanchangensis, is a polyether insecticidal antibiotic (Sun et al., 2002) and is one of the most potent hits.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sun et al., 2002

claim: NCMC has been shown to have a broad spectrum of antiviral activity against diverse arboviruses.
source: Studies of NCMC are limited, but it has been shown to have a broad spectrum of antiviral activity against diverse arboviruses (Rausch et al., 2017) and potentially SARS-CoV-2 infection (Dittmar et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Svenningsen et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rausch et al., 2017; Dittmar et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Svenningsen et al., 2020

claim: NCMC suppresses breast cancer stem cell activity and inhibits growth of breast cancer and multiple myeloma cells.
source: It also suppresses breast cancer stem cell activity and inhibits growth of breast cancer and multiple myeloma cells (Huang et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Huang et al., 2018 and Xu et al., 2020

claim: NCMC treatment significantly increased lipid droplet accumulation in primary HSC lines compared to controls.
source: We observed that NCMC treatment significantly increased lipid droplet accumulation in primary HSC lines compared to controls (Figure 2A), consistent with HSC inactivation.
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 2A showing microscopy images

claim: NCMC exhibited higher potency in HSCs from all four donors compared to nortriptyline, where 100–300 nM of NCMC exhibited similar effects on lipid droplet accumulation to 10 µM nortriptyline.
source: Compared to nortriptyline (Chen et al., 2017), NCMC exhibited higher potency in HSCs from all four donors, where 100–300 nM of NCMC exhibited similar effects on lipid droplet accumulation to 10 µM nortriptyline (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and citation to Chen et al., 2017

claim: NCMC induces lipid accumulation in both human and murine HSCs.
source: These results show that NCMC induces lipid accumulation in both human and murine HSCs.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the dose response experiments

claim: NCMC treatment reduced both ACTA2 and COL1A1 levels at 100 nM or higher in multiple primary human HSC lines.
source: NCMC treatment reduced both ACTA2 and COL1A1 levels at 100 nM or higher (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 3A–B showing qPCR data

claim: NCMC reduced Acta2 and Col1a1 expression at multiple concentrations in murine HSCs at day 2.
source: We also observed that NCMC reduced Acta2 and Col1a1 expression at multiple concentrations in murine HSCs at day 2 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 3C showing qPCR data

claim: NCMC treatment significantly decreased collagen staining intensity and fiber area in the scar-in-a-jar assay.
source: NCMC treatment significantly decreased collagen staining intensity and fiber area (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 3D–E showing microscopy images and quantification

claim: Both the basal expression of COL1A1 and TGF-β-induced COL1A1 expression were significantly reduced by NCMC treatment in spheroids consisting of primary human HSCs and primary rat hepatocytes.
source: Both the basal expression of COL1A1 and TGF-β-induced COL1A1 expression were significantly reduced by NCMC treatment (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 3F showing qPCR data from spheroids

claim: NCMC broadly affects genes associated with fibrosis as revealed by RNA-sequencing analysis.
source: HSCs were next treated with NCMC and analyzed by RNA-sequencing analysis, which revealed that NCMC broadly affects genes associated with fibrosis.
evidence: Stated as a finding from RNA-seq analysis

claim: Among the top gene sets negatively enriched in the NCMC-treated group were ECM-related signatures, including ECM structural constituent and collagen-containing ECM, as well as signatures relevant to migration, including contractile fibers.
source: Among the top gene sets negatively enriched in the NCMC-treated group were ECM-related signatures, including ECM structural constituent and collagen-containing ECM, as well as signatures relevant to migration, including contractile fibers.
evidence: Stated as a finding from GSEA analysis

claim: Genes associated with oligosaccharide lipid intermediate biosynthetic process were positively enriched in NCMC-treated cells.
source: Of note, genes associated with oligosaccharide lipid intermediate biosynthetic process were positively enriched, possibly contributing to the re-accumulation of lipid droplets (Figure 3G and Supplementary file 7).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 3G and Supplementary file 7

claim: The canonical HSC gene signature, HSC-specific signature, and liver cirrhosis signature were significantly negatively enriched in NCMC-treated cells.
source: We observed that these signatures were significantly negatively enriched (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 8).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 8

claim: Many genes that promote liver fibrosis, including those that encode collagens, TGF-β, and PDGF pathway components, are inhibited by NCMC.
source: Visualization of the canonical HSC gene signature (Zhang et al., 2016) also demonstrated that many genes that promote liver fibrosis, including those that encode collagens, TGF-β, and PDGF pathway components, are inhibited by NCMC (Figure 3H and Supplementary file 8).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 3H and Supplementary file 8, and citation to Zhang et al., 2016

claim: The mRNA level of the classic quiescent or inactivated HSC marker PPARG (PPARγ) is induced with NCMC treatment.
source: The mRNA level of the classic quiescent or inactivated HSC marker PPARG (PPARγ) is also induced with NCMC treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2 showing RNA-seq data

claim: NCMC treatment significantly reduced the number of cells that migrated through the membrane compared to DMSO controls in transwell migration assays.
source: NCMC treatment significantly reduced the number of cells that migrated through the membrane compared to DMSO controls (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 4A showing transwell migration assay results

claim: After 30 hr of treatment, the DMSO-treated control cells closed the gap in the wound healing assay, whereas the gap remained for NCMC-treated cells.
source: After 30 hr of treatment, the DMSO-treated control cells closed the gap, whereas the gap remained for NCMC-treated cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 4B showing wound healing assay results

claim: NCMC treatment reduced cell proliferation at concentrations of 25 nM and higher, and this effect on proliferation was first evident on day 2.
source: NCMC treatment reduced cell proliferation at concentrations of 25 nM and higher, and this effect on proliferation was first evident on day 2 (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 4C showing cell count data

claim: NCMC treatment only showed a small increase in the percentage of apoptotic cells in one of two donor HSC lines at 1 µM and no increase at 100 nM based on Annexin V and propidium iodide analysis.
source: Based on the analysis of Annexin V and propidium iodide (PI) by flow cytometry, NCMC treatment only showed a small increase in the percentage of apoptotic cells in one of two donor HSC lines at 1 µM and no increase at 100 nM.
evidence: Stated as a finding from flow cytometry analysis

claim: NCMC treatment increased the percentage of G0 quiescent cells based on analysis of the proliferation marker Ki-67 and PI.
source: In addition, analysis of the proliferation marker Ki-67 and PI showed that NCMC treatment increased the percentage of G0 quiescent cells (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing flow cytometry data

claim: NCMC is a polyether ionophore and has been shown to increase cytosolic Ca2+ in a cancer cell line.
source: NCMC is a polyether ionophore and has been shown to increase cytosolic Ca2+ in a cancer cell line (Huang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Huang et al., 2018

claim: At 10 µM, NCMC increased cytosolic Ca2+ in HSCs as did ionomycin and thapsigargin.
source: At 10 µM, NCMC increased cytosolic Ca2+ as did ionomycin and thapsigargin (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 4F showing calcium measurement data

claim: The increase of cytosolic Ca2+ in response to NCMC was not sensitive to EGTA, suggesting that the immediate increase of cytosolic Ca2+ following NCMC treatment is due to release of calcium from intracellular stores.
source: Similar to the effect observed with thapsigargin (Ribeiro et al., 2018), the increase of cytosolic Ca2+ in response to NCMC was not sensitive to EGTA (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), suggesting that the immediate increase of cytosolic Ca2+ following NCMC treatment is due to release of calcium from intracellular stores.
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and citation to Ribeiro et al., 2018

claim: Analysis of a dose response of NCMC demonstrated an increase in cytosolic Ca2+ at concentrations as low as 10 nM.
source: Analysis of a dose response of NCMC demonstrated an increase in cytosolic Ca2+ at concentrations as low as 10 nM (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B showing dose response data

claim: FYN phosphorylation at Y420 was reduced by approximately 40% at both 1 hr and 18 hr after NCMC treatment.
source: Among the 45 proteins tested, FYN phosphorylation at Y420 was reduced by approximately 40% at both 1 hr and 18 hr.
evidence: Stated as a finding from kinase array analysis

claim: HSPB1 (HSP27), MAPK1/3 (ERK2/1), STAT5A/B, and PTK2 (FAK) showed decreased phosphorylation at 18 hr after NCMC treatment.
source: We selected HSPB1 (HSP27), MAPK1/3 (ERK2/1), STAT5A/B, and PTK2 (FAK) to study further in addition to FYN because (1) they also showed decreased phosphorylation at 18 hr, and (2) genes encoding these products are expressed at a relatively high level in HSCs, as indicated from RNA sequencing data, suggesting that these may also be potential mechanistic targets of NCMC in HSCs.
evidence: Stated as a finding from kinase array analysis and rationale for further study

claim: Depletion of FYN, HSPB1, MAPK1, MAPK3, and STAT5B consistently reduced COL1A1 expression in human HSCs from three donors.
source: We observed a consistent reduction of COL1A1 with depletion of FYN, HSPB1, MAPK1, MAPK3, and STAT5B (Figure 5B–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that each kinase contributes to regulation of COL1A1 expression.
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 5B–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 showing qPCR data

claim: The reduction of FYN phosphorylation at Y420 was the most prominent following one hour of NCMC treatment, indicating that FYN may mediate the immediate response to NCMC in HSCs.
source: Among the kinases that consistently reduced COL1A1 expression, the reduction of FYN phosphorylation at Y420 was the most prominent following one hour of NCMC treatment, indicating that FYN may mediate the immediate response to NCMC in HSCs.
evidence: Stated as an inference from kinase array data

claim: Western blot of FYN revealed two bands – the upper band was reduced in HSCs treated with NCMC, while the lower band showed little change.
source: Western blot of FYN revealed two bands – the upper band was reduced in HSCs treated with NCMC, while the lower band showed little change (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1A showing Western blot data

claim: Both bands observed in FYN Western blot were reduced with depletion of FYN, suggesting that both products are encoded by FYN mRNA.
source: Both bands were reduced with depletion of FYN (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), suggesting that both products are encoded by FYN mRNA.
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 2 showing Western blot data

claim: qPCR analysis of NCMC-treated HSCs showed that FYN mRNA level was not affected, indicating that NCMC regulates FYN through a post transcriptional mechanism.
source: qPCR analysis of NCMC-treated HSCs showed that FYN mRNA level was not affected (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), further indicating that NCMC regulates FYN through a post transcriptional mechanism.
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 3 showing qPCR data

claim: Depletion of FYN using two different siRNA duplexes significantly reduced COL1A1 mRNA level in HSCs.
source: Both depletion of FYN using two different siRNA duplexes (Figure 6A–B) and treatment with 1-Naphthyl PP1, an inhibitor of v-Src, FYN, and ABL (Figure 6C), significantly reduced COL1A1 mRNA level in HSCs.
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 6A–B showing qPCR data

claim: Treatment with 1-Naphthyl PP1, an inhibitor of v-Src, FYN, and ABL, significantly reduced COL1A1 mRNA level in HSCs.
source: Both depletion of FYN using two different siRNA duplexes (Figure 6A–B) and treatment with 1-Naphthyl PP1, an inhibitor of v-Src, FYN, and ABL (Figure 6C), significantly reduced COL1A1 mRNA level in HSCs.
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 6C showing qPCR data

claim: Collagen deposition in the ECM was impaired by FYN depletion, as indicated by the reduced collagen intensity and fiber area in the scar-in-a-jar assay.
source: Collagen deposition in the ECM was also impaired by FYN depletion, as indicated by the reduced collagen intensity and fiber area in the scar-in-a-jar assay (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 6D showing microscopy images and quantification

claim: Ectopic expression of a dominant negative Y213A FYN mutant reduced COL1A1 expression in HSCs but did not further decrease COL1A1 level in NCMC-treated cells, suggesting that FYN inhibition is likely to be downstream of NCMC.
source: In addition, ectopic expression of a dominant negative Y213A FYN mutant (Kaspar and Jaiswal, 2011) reduced COL1A1 expression in HSCs but did not further decrease COL1A1 level in NCMC-treated cells, suggesting that FYN inhibition is likely to be downstream of NCMC (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 6E showing qPCR data and citation to Kaspar and Jaiswal, 2011

claim: Expression of dominant negative FYN in HSCs resulted in a decrease in phosphorylated MAPK, suggesting that FYN may crosstalk with the MAPK pathway to exert its function.
source: Lastly, expression of dominant negative FYN in HSCs resulted in a decrease in phosphorylated MAPK (Figure 6F), suggesting that FYN may crosstalk with the MAPK pathway to exert its function.
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 6F showing Western blot data

claim: PTK2 depletion consistently suppressed migration of HSCs isolated from three different human donors.
source: While PTK2 depletion consistently suppressed migration of HSCs isolated from three different human donors, FYN depletion only reduced migration in one HSC line (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 7A–B showing transwell migration assay results

claim: FYN depletion only reduced migration in one HSC line out of three tested.
source: While PTK2 depletion consistently suppressed migration of HSCs isolated from three different human donors, FYN depletion only reduced migration in one HSC line (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 7A–B showing transwell migration assay results

claim: Dominant negative FYN promotes phosphorylation of PTK2.
source: We also observed that dominant negative FYN promotes phosphorylation of PTK2 (Figure 6F), while NCMC reduces phosphorylation of PTK2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 4), suggesting that NCMC controls PTK2 phosphorylation and HSC migration through a pathway that is independent of FYN.
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 4 showing Western blot data

claim: NCMC reduces phosphorylation of PTK2.
source: We also observed that dominant negative FYN promotes phosphorylation of PTK2 (Figure 6F), while NCMC reduces phosphorylation of PTK2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 4), suggesting that NCMC controls PTK2 phosphorylation and HSC migration through a pathway that is independent of FYN.
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 4 showing Western blot data

claim: Depletion of MAPK1/3 consistently reduced migration across different donors.
source: Depletion of MAPK1/3 consistently reduced migration across different donors, whereas the influence of HSPB1 depletion varied across HSCs from different donors (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 7C showing transwell migration assay results

claim: The influence of HSPB1 depletion on migration varied across HSCs from different donors.
source: Depletion of MAPK1/3 consistently reduced migration across different donors, whereas the influence of HSPB1 depletion varied across HSCs from different donors (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 7C showing transwell migration assay results

claim: Dosing of 1 mg/kg NCMC every other day via intraperitoneal (IP) injection for three weeks resulted in decreased breast cancer tumor size in previous studies.
source: Previous studies showed that dosing of 1 mg/kg every other day via intraperitoneal (IP) injection for three weeks resulted in decreased breast cancer tumor size (Huang et al., 2018), and that oral administration of 2 mg/kg or 4 mg/kg NCMC daily for 20 days reduces multiple myeloma subcutaneous xenografts in nude mice without affecting liver functions, as indicated by aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels (Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Huang et al., 2018

claim: Oral administration of 2 mg/kg or 4 mg/kg NCMC daily for 20 days reduces multiple myeloma subcutaneous xenografts in nude mice without affecting liver functions.
source: Previous studies showed that dosing of 1 mg/kg every other day via intraperitoneal (IP) injection for three weeks resulted in decreased breast cancer tumor size (Huang et al., 2018), and that oral administration of 2 mg/kg or 4 mg/kg NCMC daily for 20 days reduces multiple myeloma subcutaneous xenografts in nude mice without affecting liver functions, as indicated by aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels (Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xu et al., 2020

claim: A single dose of 1 mg/kg NCMC via IP injection resulted in a maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) of 108±39.7 nM reached at 4 hr followed by a decrease to less than 50 nM after 12 hr.
source: The maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) of 108±39.7 nM was reached at 4 hr followed by a decrease to less than 50 nM after 12 hr.
evidence: Stated as a finding from pharmacokinetic studies

claim: The terminal elimination half-life (t1/2) of NCMC was estimated to be 5.7±0.87 hr.
source: Based on the analysis of plasma concentration over time, we estimated a terminal elimination half-life (t1/2) of 5.7±0.87 hr.
evidence: Stated as a finding from pharmacokinetic studies

claim: The calculated volume of distribution (Vss/F) is nearly 10 L/kg, indicating substantial distribution into tissue.
source: As anticipated from the flat concentration-time curve, the calculated volume of distribution (Vss/F) is nearly 10 L/kg, indicating substantial distribution into tissue.
evidence: Stated as a finding from pharmacokinetic studies

claim: After 4 days of daily IP dosing at 1 mg/kg, 10-fold higher NCMC concentration was detected in fat tissue compared to plasma, whereas it was undetectable in liver and muscle.
source: We detected 10-fold higher NCMC concentration in fat tissue compared to plasma, whereas it was undetectable in liver and muscle.
evidence: Stated as a finding from pharmacokinetic studies

claim: The fraction of NCMC bound to serum proteins was measured at >99%.
source: The trough total plasma concentration was in the range of EC50 in cell culture, which would result in a lower effective concentration when taking into consideration the fraction of NCMC bound to serum proteins, which we measured at >99% (the reported plasma concentrations refer to the total = free + bound plasma concentrations).
evidence: Stated as a finding from pharmacokinetic studies

claim: Hepatic microsomes from mice showed evidence of degradation of NCMC by phase I liver metabolism, as indicated by the short half-life (37.8 min) and high derived intrinsic clearance (36.7 µl/min/mg protein).
source: Further, hepatic microsomes from mice showed evidence of degradation of NCMC by phase I liver metabolism, as indicated by the short half-life (37.8 min) and high derived intrinsic clearance (36.7 µl/min/mg protein).
evidence: Stated as a finding from microsome analysis

claim: The pharmacokinetic data suggest that NCMC will not reach sufficient exposure in the liver to achieve hepatic antifibrotic effects in vivo.
source: In summary, the pharmacokinetic data suggest that NCMC will not reach sufficient exposure in the liver to achieve hepatic antifibrotic effects in vivo.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from pharmacokinetic studies

claim: The degree of fibrosis is the strongest predictive factor for liver-related mortality.
source: Liver fibrosis is the major driver of liver failure in all etiologies of chronic liver disease, and the degree of fibrosis is the strongest predictive factor for liver-related mortality (Anstee et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Anstee et al., 2019

claim: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease affects one in four people worldwide.
source: However, there is a lack of effective treatment for several chronic liver diseases, such as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, which affects one in four people worldwide (Younossi et al., 2016), and primary sclerosing cholangitis (Karlsen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Younossi et al., 2016

claim: The scarring process in the liver is reversible.
source: With evidence that the scarring process in the liver is reversible (Sun et al., 2020) and that HSC myofibroblasts demonstrate plasticity and can revert to an inactive state (Kisseleva et al., 2012; Troeger et al., 2012), there is increasing enthusiasm for development of approaches to promote HSC inactivation as a therapeutic strategy to treat liver fibrosis.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sun et al., 2020

claim: Lipid droplet re-accumulation is recognized as a feature of quiescent and inactivated HSCs.
source: First, although lipid droplet re-accumulation is recognized as a feature of quiescent and inactivated HSCs (Zisser et al., 2021), it is possible that partially inactivated HSCs may not accumulate enough lipid droplets to pass our primary screen cutoff, and therefore compounds that act to reduce collagen expression or other fibrosis-related aspects of HSCs without affecting lipid accumulation may be missed in this screen.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zisser et al., 2021

claim: Polyether ionophores demonstrate antibacterial, antifungal, antiparasitic, antimalarial, antiviral, anti-inflammatory activities and cytotoxicity in cancer cells.
source: This group of compounds demonstrates antibacterial, antifungal, antiparasitic, antimalarial, antiviral, anti-inflammatory activities and cytotoxicity in cancer cells (Kevin Ii et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kevin Ii et al., 2009

claim: NCMC demonstrated substantial cytotoxicity in cell culture at concentrations higher than 10 µM.
source: Indeed, we observe that NCMC demonstrated substantial cytotoxicity in cell culture at concentrations higher than 10 µM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing cell count data

claim: The EC50 of NCMC in lipid accumulation assay is in the range of 10–300 nM without inducing apoptosis.
